title: Agile, Scrum and Jira
tagline: Work in short cycles, deliver value early and keep improving, with practice in every module
summary: Learn agile ways of working: values and principles, the Scrum framework, user stories and backlogs, estimating and forecasting, boards and metrics, retrospectives and team health. Includes how to use work-tracking tools such as Jira sensibly. Every module has a hands-on lab.

modules.title: Agile foundations
modules.summary: Why agile exists, what its values and principles say and how it differs from plan-driven delivery.
modules.outcome: You can explain the agile values, compare agile with plan-driven approaches and describe the cycle of iterative delivery.
modules.intro: Agile is a way of working that favours learning, small steps and close collaboration over big plans. It began in software but is now used across marketing, product, education and operations.

topics.title: Why agile?
topics.html:
Traditional plan-driven projects try to define everything first, then build, then deliver at the end. That works when requirements are stable, but when users cannot fully describe what they need, or the world changes, the end result may arrive late and be wrong.

A comparison
Plan-drivenAgile
PlanningDetailed up frontContinuous, in short cycles
DeliveryOne big release at the endSmall usable pieces often
FeedbackAt the endAfter every cycle
ChangeCostly and controlledExpected and welcomed
RiskDiscovered lateReduced by early learning

The bars are illustrative, not data from a study, but they show the idea: agile aims to move surprises earlier, when they are cheap to fix.

Tip

Agile is not 'no plan'. It is planning enough to start, then learning and re-planning often.

Picture a team asked to build an app for a college library. A plan-driven team would spend two months writing a specification, three months building, and then show the finished app to students in month six. If the students then say they would rather reserve books from their phones than search on a desktop page, much of the work has to be redone. An agile team builds a simple search in the first fortnight, puts it in front of students, learns about phones in week two and adjusts the next fortnight's work. The total effort may be similar, but the risk of building the wrong thing is far smaller because learning happens while there is still time to change course.

Check what you just learned

1. Agile favours:
  • One big release
  • Small increments with feedback (correct)
  • No planning
  • Long documents

Learn early and often.
keyPoints: Agile delivers small pieces often and learns from feedback.
It moves surprises earlier, when they are cheaper.

topics.title: Values and principles
topics.html:
Definition

The Agile Manifesto. A short statement of values written in 2001 by seventeen software practitioners. It prefers some things over others, while still valuing the items on the right.

The four values
We value moreOver
Individuals and interactionsProcesses and tools
Working softwareComprehensive documentation
Customer collaborationContract negotiation
Responding to changeFollowing a plan

Key principles (paraphrased)

  • Satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery.
  • Welcome changing requirements, even late.
  • Deliver working product frequently, from weeks to a couple of months.
  • Business people and developers work together daily.
  • Build projects around motivated individuals and trust them.
  • Working product is the primary measure of progress.
  • Maintain a sustainable pace.
  • Reflect regularly and adjust.
Watch out

The manifesto does not say documentation, plans or contracts are bad. It says the items on the left are valued more when there is a trade-off.

Check what you just learned

1. The manifesto values working software over:
  • Teamwork
  • Customers
  • Comprehensive documentation (correct)
  • Change

Documentation still matters but is secondary.
keyPoints: Four values prefer people, working product, collaboration and responding to change.
The right-hand items still have value.

topics.title: Frameworks and mindset
topics.html:
Common approaches
ApproachIdeaGood for
ScrumFixed-length sprints with defined roles and eventsProduct development with a team
KanbanVisualise work and limit work in progress; continuous flowSupport, operations, steady streams
Extreme ProgrammingTechnical practices such as pair programming and test-driven developmentSoftware quality
LeanRemove waste, deliver value quicklyProcess improvement
Scaled frameworksCoordinate many teamsLarge organisations

Frameworks are tools. Agile is a mindset: curiosity, collaboration, transparency, willingness to adapt. A team can run every Scrum event and still not be agile if it ignores feedback or hides problems.

Agile mindset habits

  • Make work visible.
  • Inspect and adapt.
  • Prefer experiments to opinions.
  • Share ownership of the outcome.
  • Value learning, including from failure.
Tip

When a practice feels pointless, ask what problem it was meant to solve, rather than simply dropping or defending it.

Check what you just learned

1. Kanban focuses on:
  • Fixed sprints
  • Contracts
  • Long plans
  • Visualising work and limiting work in progress (correct)

It manages flow.

Key terms: flip and sort

Agile
An approach based on iteration and feedback
Increment
A usable piece of product
Iteration
A repeated short cycle
Kanban
A flow-based method using a visual board
Mindset
Beliefs that shape behaviour
keyPoints: Scrum, Kanban, XP and Lean are tools; agile is a mindset.
Choose practices by the problem they solve.

modules.title: The Scrum framework
modules.summary: Understand Scrum's accountabilities, events and artifacts, and how they work together.
modules.outcome: You can describe the Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers, the five events and the three artifacts with their commitments.
modules.intro: Scrum is a lightweight framework for developing and sustaining complex products. It is simple to understand and hard to master, because it asks teams to be honest about what is really happening.

topics.title: Roles in Scrum
topics.html:
Three accountabilities
RoleAccountable forNot the same as
Product OwnerMaximising the value of the product; managing the backlogA project manager who assigns tasks
Scrum MasterThe team's use of Scrum and its effectiveness; removing impedimentsA boss or administrator
DevelopersCreating a usable increment each sprintJust programmers: all who do the work

Together these form the Scrum Team: a small, cross-functional group, typically ten or fewer people, with all the skills needed to deliver the product. The team is self-managing: it decides internally who does what and how.

What each role does day to day

  • Product Owner: talks to users and stakeholders, writes and orders backlog items, decides what 'done' means for value.
  • Scrum Master: coaches, facilitates events, protects the team from distractions, helps with blockers.
  • Developers: plan the sprint, build, test, and inspect their own progress daily.

Common mistakes

  • The Product Owner is a committee.
  • The Scrum Master acts as a manager who assigns work.
  • Developers wait to be told how to do their work.

Check what you just learned

1. Who orders the product backlog?
  • The Product Owner (correct)
  • The Scrum Master
  • The Developers alone
  • Management

The PO is accountable for it.
keyPoints: Product Owner owns value, Scrum Master supports Scrum, Developers build the increment.
The team is small, cross-functional and self-managing.

topics.title: The five events
topics.html:
The events
EventPurposeTime-box for a one-month sprint
SprintA fixed-length container of one month or less in which work is done1 month or less
Sprint PlanningChoose what to deliver and how; create the sprint goalUp to 8 hours
Daily ScrumInspect progress towards the goal and adapt the plan15 minutes
Sprint ReviewShow the increment to stakeholders and get feedbackUp to 4 hours
Sprint RetrospectiveInspect how we worked and plan improvementsUp to 3 hours

For shorter sprints the events are usually shorter. A two-week sprint often has planning of about four hours, a review of two hours and a retrospective of 90 minutes.

Watch out

The Daily Scrum is for the Developers to coordinate. It is not a status meeting for managers.

Time-boxes matter because they force choices. A planning meeting with no limit tends to expand to fill the day, while a limit pushes the team to decide what is most important and to defer the rest. Similarly, a fixed sprint length makes the team's rhythm predictable for everyone around it: stakeholders know when the next review will happen, and the team learns how much it can finish in that time. Changing the sprint length every few weeks removes this benefit, so teams usually choose a length, try it for several sprints and adjust only after reflecting in a retrospective.

Check what you just learned

1. The Sprint Retrospective inspects:
  • The product
  • How the team worked (correct)
  • The budget
  • Customer contracts

Process improvement.
keyPoints: Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Review and Retrospective happen within a Sprint.
Time-boxes keep events focused.

topics.title: Artifacts and commitments
topics.html:
Artifacts and their commitments
ArtifactWhat it isCommitment
Product BacklogAn ordered list of everything needed in the productProduct Goal
Sprint BacklogThe items chosen for this sprint plus the plan to deliver themSprint Goal
IncrementA concrete, usable step towards the product goalDefinition of Done
Definition

Definition of Done. A shared, written standard that an item must meet to count as finished, for example: reviewed, tested, documented and demonstrated.

Worked example

A sprint goal

A library app team in sprint 1.

  1. Goal: students can log in and search the catalogue by title.
  2. Selected stories support the goal.
  3. If a story must be dropped, the team keeps the goal and renegotiates scope with the Product Owner.

Answer. A goal gives the team flexibility and purpose.

Tip

An item that is 'almost done' is not done. Only finished work creates value and information.

Check what you just learned

1. The Definition of Done applies to:
  • Meetings
  • The budget
  • The Increment (correct)
  • The roles

It is the quality bar for finished work.

Key terms: flip and sort

Sprint
A fixed-length period for delivering an increment
Product Backlog
The ordered list of product work
Sprint Goal
The purpose of the sprint
Definition of Done
The shared quality standard
Impediment
A blocker
keyPoints: Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment.
Each has a commitment: Product Goal, Sprint Goal, Definition of Done.

modules.title: Requirements and the backlog
modules.summary: Write user stories, add acceptance criteria and order a backlog by value.
modules.outcome: You can write user stories, check them against INVEST, add acceptance criteria and prioritise by value and effort.
modules.intro: The backlog is the team's list of everything that might be built. Its quality largely decides the quality of the product. Good stories are short conversations plus clear conditions of satisfaction.

topics.title: User stories
topics.html:
Formula · The story form

As a <type of user>, I want <a goal> so that <a reason>

As a student, I want to reserve a book so that I get it when it is returned.

INVEST: a checklist for good stories

  • Independent: can be built in any order where possible.
  • Negotiable: details are discussed, not fixed in stone.
  • Valuable: matters to a user or the business.
  • Estimable: the team can size it.
  • Small: fits within a sprint.
  • Testable: you can tell when it is done.
Poor to good
PoorBetter
Make the app betterAs a student, I want to see book availability in search results so that I do not walk to the library for nothing
Build the entire library systemA series of small stories: search, reserve, view loans
Use a database(a technical task inside a story, not a story)
Tip

A story is a promise of a conversation. The card is short; the detail is discussed with the Product Owner and tested by the criteria.

Stories should also be sliced vertically rather than horizontally. A horizontal slice delivers one technical layer, such as 'build the database', which no user can see or test. A vertical slice cuts through every layer to deliver a thin but usable piece of behaviour, such as 'a student can search by title and see a result'. Vertical slices give feedback sooner and make progress visible. When a story feels too big, ask whether there is a simpler version a user could try this week, and make that the first story.

Check what you just learned

1. The 'so that' part of a story explains:
  • The technology
  • The cost
  • The deadline
  • The value or reason (correct)

It states the benefit.
keyPoints: Write 'As a, I want, so that' stories.
Check them against INVEST.

topics.title: Acceptance criteria and Definition of Done
topics.html:
Acceptance criteria are conditions that a specific story must satisfy to be accepted. They remove ambiguity and guide testing.

Two formats
FormatExample
ChecklistSearch results show in under 3 seconds; each result shows in or out
Given-when-thenGiven I am logged in, when I search for 'Physics', then I see a list of matching books with their status

Good criteria are

  • Testable: pass or fail, no opinions.
  • Specific: numbers where it matters.
  • Short: three to six per story.
  • Written from the user's view.
  • Agreed before work starts.
Acceptance criteria and Definition of Done
Acceptance criteriaDefinition of Done
Applies toOne storyEvery story
ContentWhat this story must doQuality bar: reviewed, tested, documented
Set byProduct Owner with the teamThe team and organisation

Check what you just learned

1. Which is better acceptance criteria?
  • Search results appear in under 3 seconds (correct)
  • The search should be fast
  • It is nice
  • Search works well

It is measurable.
keyPoints: Acceptance criteria are testable conditions for a story.
The Definition of Done is a shared quality bar for all stories.

topics.title: Prioritising the backlog
topics.html:
The Product Owner orders the backlog so the most valuable and urgent work is at the top. Items near the top are small and well understood; items at the bottom can stay vague.

Ordering methods
MethodIdea
Value versus effortDo high-value, low-effort items first
MoSCoWMust, Should, Could, Won't (this time)
Cost of delayPrioritise work that loses most value if delayed
Risk firstTackle the riskiest assumptions early
KanoBalance basics, performance and delighters

Value per point

Change value and effort to see which items rise to the top.

Adjust Value (1-100), Effort (story points) and see Value per point, Points affordable with 20 points of capacity change.

Backlog hygiene

  • Refine regularly: split large items, clarify details.
  • Remove items no longer wanted.
  • Keep the top of the backlog ready for planning.
  • Be honest about what will never be built.

Check what you just learned

1. MoSCoW's M stands for:
  • Maybe
  • Must (correct)
  • More
  • Money

M means Must have: essential for this release.

Key terms: flip and sort

User story
A short description of a need from a user's view
INVEST
A checklist for good stories
Acceptance criteria
Conditions a story must meet
Refinement
Clarifying and splitting backlog items
MoSCoW
Must, should, could, won't
keyPoints: Order by value, urgency, risk and effort.
Refine regularly.

modules.title: Planning, estimating and forecasting
modules.summary: Estimate relative size, use velocity and forecast delivery honestly.
modules.outcome: You can size stories in points, calculate velocity and give a range-based forecast.
modules.intro: Agile teams estimate to plan, not to promise. They prefer relative sizes and ranges, and they use their own history rather than hope.

topics.title: Story points and relative sizing
topics.html:
Humans are poor at estimating absolute time but fairly good at comparing things. A story point is a unit of relative size that blends effort, complexity and uncertainty. A 5-point story is larger than a 3-point story, roughly 1.67 times as big.

A common sequence
PointsMeaning
1Very small and well understood
2Small
3Medium
5Moderate, some uncertainty
8Large; consider splitting
13Very large; split before planning

Why this works

  • Private choice avoids anchoring.
  • Differences reveal different assumptions.
  • Discussion shares knowledge.
  • Relative sizes are quicker than hours.

Common mistakes

  • Turning points into hours.
  • Comparing teams' points.
  • Using points to judge individual performance.

Check what you just learned

1. Story points measure:
  • Hours exactly
  • Salary
  • Relative size (correct)
  • Importance

Effort, complexity and uncertainty.
keyPoints: Points are relative size, not hours.
Planning poker exposes assumptions.

topics.title: Velocity and forecasting
topics.html:
Definition

Velocity. The number of story points a team completes in a sprint. It is an observation of past performance, used for forecasting, not a target.

An example
SprintPoints done
118
222
320
424
521
Formula · Forecast

sprints needed = remaining points / velocity (round up)

Remaining 120 points at average velocity 21 gives about 6 sprints; at the lowest velocity 18 about 7; at the highest 24 about 5.

Giving a range such as 'five to seven sprints, most likely six' is more honest and more useful than a single date.

Watch out

Never use velocity to compare teams or to pressure a team. Points mean different things in different teams, and pressure leads to inflated estimates.

Check what you just learned

1. Velocity is:
  • A target
  • A quality score
  • A salary
  • An observation of past output (correct)

Use it to forecast.
keyPoints: Velocity is the average points per sprint.
Forecast with a range.

topics.title: Sprint Planning in practice
topics.html:
Before planning

  1. The backlog is refined at the top.
  2. The team knows its capacity (holidays, support work).
  3. The Product Owner has a draft goal.
Capacity
ItemExample
Team size4 people
Working days in sprint10
Average velocity21 points
Planned absence2 days (one person)
Adjusted capacityabout 17 to 19 points
Tip

Plan slightly under capacity. A team that regularly finishes early can pull more work; a team that regularly misses its goals loses trust and morale.

Check what you just learned

1. Planning slightly under capacity helps:
  • Build trust by meeting goals (correct)
  • Waste time
  • Avoid stories
  • Skip reviews

Reliable delivery matters.

Key terms: flip and sort

Story point
A relative unit of size
Velocity
Points completed per sprint
Capacity
Work the team can take on
Planning poker
A group estimating game
Forecast
An estimate with a range
keyPoints: Plan: why, what, how.
Adjust capacity for absence and plan slightly under.

modules.title: Boards, metrics and tracker tools
modules.summary: Visualise work on boards, read burndown and flow metrics and use tracker tools such as Jira sensibly.
modules.outcome: You can design a board, apply WIP limits, read a burndown chart and describe common tracker concepts.
modules.intro: Agile makes work visible. Boards and charts show where work is stuck and whether the team is on course. Tools like Jira help, but they are only as good as the habits behind them.

topics.title: Boards and flow
topics.html:
A board shows each item as a card moving across columns. At a glance anyone can see what is being worked on, what is blocked and what has finished.

Kanban practices that help any team

  • Limit work in progress (WIP): finish before starting.
  • Make policies explicit: what 'Done' means for each column.
  • Track how long items take from start to finish (cycle time).
  • Look for bottlenecks: columns where cards pile up.
  • Improve regularly.
Why WIP limits help
Without limitsWith limits
Many items started, few finishedFewer started, more finished
Long waits and context switchingFaster flow
Hidden bottlenecksBottlenecks show quickly
Tip

If cards pile up in 'In review', the fix is not to start more work; it is to review faster.

Check what you just learned

1. A WIP limit encourages teams to:
  • Start more work
  • Finish before starting (correct)
  • Skip reviews
  • Delete cards

Focus on completion.
keyPoints: Boards make work visible.
WIP limits improve flow and expose bottlenecks.

topics.title: Burndown and other metrics
topics.html:
Useful metrics
MetricShowsCaution
Sprint burndownRemaining work through the sprintLook at trend, not daily wiggles
VelocityPoints per sprintNot a target
Cycle timeDays from start to doneWatch for long tails
ThroughputItems finished per periodDepends on item size
Defect rateBugs found after releaseUse to improve, not to blame
Formula · Ideal burndown

ideal remaining on day d = starting points - (starting points / sprint days) × d

With 40 points over 5 days: day 1 = 32, day 2 = 24, day 3 = 16.

Watch out

Measure to learn, not to judge. When a metric becomes a target, people change behaviour to improve the number rather than the product.

Check what you just learned

1. A burndown chart shows:
  • Bugs only
  • Team salaries
  • Remaining work over time (correct)
  • Meetings

Is the sprint on course?
keyPoints: Burndown, velocity, cycle time and throughput each answer a different question.
Measure to learn, not to judge.

topics.title: Using Jira and similar tools well
topics.html:
Common concepts
ConceptMeaning
IssueAny tracked piece of work
EpicA large body of work grouping many stories
StoryA user-focused item
Task / sub-taskTechnical or smaller work
BugA defect
SprintA time-boxed iteration containing chosen issues
BoardA visual workflow of columns
WorkflowThe allowed states and transitions
BacklogThe list of upcoming issues

Habits that keep a tool useful

  • Keep issue titles short and clear.
  • Keep the board current; update cards daily.
  • Use labels and epics sparingly.
  • Do not let the tool replace conversation.
  • Review and clean the backlog regularly.
  • Remember that the tool supports the team, not the other way round.

Common mistakes

  • Creating hundreds of tiny issues nobody reads.
  • Using the tool to control people.
  • Hiding problems by not updating cards.

Tools differ, and the names above are those commonly used in work trackers such as Jira. If your organisation uses a different tool, the same concepts apply under similar names.

Check what you just learned

1. An epic is:
  • A meeting
  • A single bug
  • A person
  • A large body of work grouping stories (correct)

It groups related work.

Key terms: flip and sort

WIP limit
A cap on items in progress
Cycle time
Time from start to finish
Throughput
Items finished per period
Burndown
Remaining work over time
Epic
A large body of work
keyPoints: Issue, epic, story, task, bug, sprint, board.
Tools support conversation; they do not replace it.

modules.title: Teams, improvement and scaling
modules.summary: Build healthy teams, run useful retrospectives and know the limits of agile.
modules.outcome: You can run a retrospective, identify common anti-patterns and decide when agile is a good fit.
modules.intro: Agile works when people trust each other and improve steadily. This final module covers the human side: teamwork, retrospectives, common failures and when to scale or not.

topics.title: Healthy agile teams
topics.html:
Signs of a healthy team

  • People speak up, including to disagree.
  • Mistakes are discussed openly, without blame.
  • The team owns its commitments.
  • Work is shared, not siloed.
  • Meetings are short and useful.
  • The pace is sustainable.
Team stages (Tuckman)
StageWhat it feels like
FormingPolite, uncertain
StormingConflict about roles and methods
NormingAgreements and trust grow
PerformingSmooth collaboration

Storming is normal and not a sign of failure. Good facilitation helps the team move through it. Psychological safety, the belief that you will not be punished for speaking up, is the strongest predictor of high-performing teams in the research published by several large organisations.

Tip

Start meetings with a quick check-in. It builds connection, and people speak more easily later.

Check what you just learned

1. Psychological safety means:
  • People can speak up without fear (correct)
  • Safe buildings
  • No conflict ever
  • Security guards

Trust to speak.
keyPoints: Healthy teams are open, share ownership and pace themselves.
Psychological safety enables learning.

topics.title: Retrospectives that work
topics.html:
Formats
FormatQuestions
Start / Stop / ContinueWhat should we start, stop and continue?
Went well / To improve / ActionsSimple and widely used
SailboatWhat is the wind, the anchor, the rocks?
4LsLiked, Learned, Lacked, Longed for

Making retros useful

  1. Pick one or two improvements, not ten.
  2. Give each action an owner and a date.
  3. Review last retro's actions first.
  4. Rotate facilitation and formats.
  5. Keep it safe: focus on process, not people.

Common mistakes

  • Complaining without actions.
  • Repeating the same retro every time.
  • Not following up.

Check what you just learned

1. A retro should end with:
  • Blame
  • Owned actions (correct)
  • Nothing
  • A long list of complaints

Improvement needs commitment.
keyPoints: Retros produce one or two owned improvements.
Follow up on last time's actions.

topics.title: When agile fits, and when it does not
topics.html:
Good fit and poor fit
Fits wellFits less well
Uncertain needsFixed, well-understood requirements
Users available for feedbackNo access to users
Work can be split into small piecesWork that cannot be delivered in parts (a single physical bridge)
Motivated, skilled teamRigid, low-trust culture
Change is likely and valuableStrict regulatory sequence of approvals

Even where full Scrum does not fit, agile ideas often help: short feedback loops, visible work, regular reflection. Many organisations use hybrids.

Common agile anti-patterns

  • Agile as 'do everything faster'.
  • Sprints used as mini-waterfalls.
  • A Product Owner who is never available.
  • Managers who assign tasks inside the sprint.
  • No Definition of Done.
  • Velocity used as a performance score.
Watch out

Be wary of promises that agile will fix an unhealthy organisation by itself. It makes problems visible; people still have to fix them.

Check what you just learned

1. Agile is likely to fit poorly when:
  • Requirements are unclear
  • Users are available
  • Work is fixed and cannot be delivered in parts (correct)
  • Change is expected

Not every project fits.

Key terms: flip and sort

Psychological safety
Belief that speaking up is safe
Retrospective
A review of how the team worked
Anti-pattern
A common but harmful practice
Hybrid
A mix of agile and plan-driven methods
keyPoints: Agile fits uncertain, splittable work with feedback.
It exposes problems; it does not solve them alone.
